newsitem.title: HUNGARY: PHILIP EXPRESSES CONCERN OVER DANUBE DAM EFFECTS.
newsitem.headline: PHILIP EXPRESSES CONCERN OVER DANUBE DAM EFFECTS.

text.p: Britain's Prince Philip expressed concern on Tuesday over the negative environmental effects of the Danube dam which is currently the subject of a court dispute between Hungary and Slovakia.

"We've established what effects the development has had on the area and it is of course very worrying," Philip told reporters on a visit to Hungary in his role as Honorary President of the Worldwide Fund for Nature (WWF).

Hungary is currently pleading its case at the International Court of Justice in the Hague against Slovakia's unilateral diversion of the Danube along a man-made navigation canal in 1992 to fuel a vast hydro-electric plant at Gabcikovo.
The Slovak dam was originally part of a 1977 plan agreed by the then Communist governments of Czechoslovakia and Hungary.
But Hungary suspended work on a companion dam downstream at Nagymaros in 1989 following pressure from environmental groups, and in 1992 it pulled out of the project altogether.

Slovakia says Hungary broke its part of the agreement and should therefore pay damages to Slovakia, arguing that Budapest made the environmental problems worse by halting construction of the Nagymaros dam which would have offset the effects of Gabcikovo.

Hungarian Foreign Ministry lawyer Gyorgy Szenasi told the International Court on Monday the project was an illegal act of "self-enrichment" which was wreaking havoc on the environment and depriving Hungarians of vital water resources.
"These acts were a serious violation of the territorial sovereignty of Hungary," he sad.
At the end of 1995 the WWF said the scheme had caused ground water levels to drop by up to three metres (10 feet) and was threatening up to 90 percent of the marshy region's rich plant and wildlife.
The WWF added that an underground area of 14,000 cubic metres of water-filled gravel containing Europe's best and largest drinking water reserve was threatened with pollution.
Philip said on Tuesday the WWF would provide help in carrying out any environmental projects resulting from the Hague court's decisions.
"We don't know what the judgement will be but I think it is quite sure that the WWF will do what it can to (help) meet that judgement," he said.
Philip was in Hungary on the first leg of a tour of a dozen countrie to raise funds for the WWF.
On Monday he witnessed the introduction of a five-member family of Austrian beavers to one of Europe's last remaining natural flood forests in Europe at Gemenc in southern Hungary.
